title: Total property tax exemption for a disabled Veteran
summary: Puerto Rico exempts the home of a disabled Veteran from property tax entirely, along with the lot up to 1,000 square metres in an urban zone or one cuerda in a rural one. Build, buy or remodel all qualify.
amount: Full exemption from payment of property taxes on the house, plus the lot up to 1,000 square metres in urban zones or one cuerda in rural zones
eligibility: You are a disabled or impaired Veteran, which the law calls a veterano incapacitado o impedido
The house was built, acquired or remodeled by you, or will be built, acquired or remodeled by you in the future
The property is the residence of you or your immediate family
The land exemption is capped at 1,000 square metres in urban zones, or one cuerda in rural zones
details: A cuerda is the Puerto Rican land measure, about 3,930 square metres, so just under an acre. In a rural zone the land allowance is therefore roughly four times the urban one.

Remodelling counts, and so does future work. The provision covers a house already built, acquired or remodeled and one you build, acquire or remodel later, so a Veteran planning a move or a renovation is not shut out.
The exemption is tied to the home being lived in. It ceases as soon as the property stops being used as the residence of the Veteran or their immediate family.

But losing it is not permanent, and this is the important part. The right to the exemption is recoverable once you rebuild your home on the previously exempt property, or acquire another property and establish your home there. So selling up or being displaced does not end the benefit for good.

The statute attributes the provision to a federal Act effective 1 January 1968, which the published text cites as Congress Act 06-89 and marks with sic. That citation looks garbled in the official compilation, so do not spend time chasing it.
This exemption sits alongside the general Veteran exemption, not instead of it. The law states that the general exemption is in addition to any other exemption Puerto Rico grants taxpayers.

Applications go to the Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales, known as CRIM, which is the body that collects municipal property tax across Puerto Rico. Its Executive Director issues the regulations and determines how claims are made. CRIM's online services list an exención de veterano among the applications you can file electronically.

On currency: the version of the law we read is the Office of Management and Budget compilation revised 3 August 2026, which carries the amendments made in 2025 and 2026. That is about as current as a published compilation gets.
agency: Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (CRIM)
statuteRef: Ley 203-2007, Carta de Derechos del Veterano Puertorriqueño del Siglo XXI, Article C, Segundo (b)

title: General Veteran property tax exemption, and why the $50,000 figure is wrong now
summary: Every Veteran in Puerto Rico gets a permanent property tax exemption on their principal residence, with no disability required. The amount is $5,000 of assessed value. It was $50,000 for ten fiscal years ending in 2018-19, and a lot of guidance still quotes that.
amount: $5,000 of assessed value, permanently. The figure was $50,000 for the fiscal years 2009-10 through 2018-19 only
eligibility: You are a Veteran, or the surviving spouse of a Veteran. No disability is required
The dwelling was built or acquired in good faith as your principal residence

Where the building contains more than one dwelling, the exempt value is the proportional part of the total value of the building and lot attributable to the dwelling you occupy, as determined by the Executive Director of CRIM
You apply in the form CRIM determines
details: Check any figure you have been given against the dates. The statute sets the permanent exemption at $5,000 of assessed value, and then lists ten specific fiscal years, 2009-10 through 2018-19, for which it was $50,000. That enhanced period has ended. Guidance written during it, or copied from guidance written during it, overstates the benefit tenfold.
The exemption is permanent and requires no disability, which makes it the one benefit here that every Veteran who owns a home in Puerto Rico should be claiming.

It stacks. The law says expressly that this exemption is in addition to any other exemption the Commonwealth grants to taxpayers, so it sits on top of the ordinary residential exoneración rather than replacing it. A disabled Veteran should look at the total exemption record as well.

Backdating is allowed, and this is worth money. Once an application is approved its effect is retroactive, up to a maximum of three years. If you have owned your home as a Veteran for years without claiming, apply anyway and ask about the three years.

The retroactivity is subject to the municipal law, which the published text still cites as Ley 81 of 30 August 1991. A note in the compilation records that this was repealed and replaced by Ley 107-2020, the Código Municipal de Puerto Rico. Expect CRIM to work from the newer code.

Vivienda, the word for dwelling, is defined to include the building where you have established your principal residence and that of your immediate family, together with the lot it sits on. In a multi-unit building it covers only the part you actually occupy as your home.

Surviving family are protected beyond the spouse. Article 6 of the law continues the privileges and exemptions for the surviving spouse, for minor children, and for adult children who are incapacitated, for as long as the Veteran would have enjoyed them. They end for a spouse on remarriage, for minor children on reaching majority, and for incapacitated children when the incapacity ends after majority.

CRIM's public frequently asked questions cover the ordinary residential exoneración and agricultural exemptions but not the Veteran exemption, so do not take its absence there as a sign the benefit does not exist. Its own services page lists the exención de veterano as an electronic filing.
agency: Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (CRIM)
statuteRef: Ley 203-2007, Article C, Segundo (a), with surviving family at Article 6, 29 L.P.R.A. 739

title: A $1,500 Veteran deduction on your Puerto Rico return
summary: Every Veteran is entitled to a $1,500 deduction under the Puerto Rico Internal Revenue Code. Ask Hacienda to confirm how it applies to your year, because the statute's wording leaves that open.
amount: $1,500, described in the statute as a deducción vitalicia, a lifetime deduction
eligibility: You are a Veteran, as defined by Article 5 of the Veterans Bill of Rights
The deduction has been effective since the tax year beginning 1 January 2007
The Secretary of the Treasury is empowered to issue the rules and regulations governing it
details: We are flagging a genuine ambiguity rather than resolving it for you. The statute grants a deducción vitalicia, literally a lifetime deduction, of $1,500. That phrasing does not say on its face whether the $1,500 is available in each year for the rest of your life or is a single allowance. We are not going to guess at a number that goes on your tax return.

Ask the Departamento de Hacienda, and ask by citation. The deduction was originally keyed to Section 1023(bb)(4) of the 1994 Internal Revenue Code, and the compilation notes it has been substituted by Section 1033.18(a)(2) of Ley 1-2011, the Puerto Rico Internal Revenue Code of 2011. Quote that section and you will get a straight answer.

The Secretary of the Treasury is authorised to promulgate rules and regulations about the deduction, and the statute says those have the force of law once approved, so the practical answer may live in a regulation rather than in the statute.

Note what this is not. It is not an exemption of military retirement pay. Puerto Rico's treatment of military retirement income is a separate question under the Internal Revenue Code of 2011 and we have not verified it, so do not assume your retired pay is exempt because this deduction exists.

Puerto Rico's income tax is its own system, not a mirror of the federal one. If you are moving to Puerto Rico from a state, that is the single biggest thing to get professional advice about, and it is worth more than this deduction either way.
The source is the Office of Management and Budget compilation of Ley 203-2007 revised 3 August 2026, which carries the 2025 and 2026 amendments.
agency: Departamento de Hacienda de Puerto Rico
statuteRef: Ley 203-2007, Article C, Primero, applying Section 1033.18(a)(2) of Ley 1-2011

title: Free tuition at the University of Puerto Rico, including if you have no GI Bill left
summary: Puerto Rico gives Veterans free tuition at the University of Puerto Rico and every public postsecondary institution, both when your federal education benefits run out mid-degree and when you never had any. The university is barred from asking for extra paperwork.
amount: Free tuition at the University of Puerto Rico and all its academic units, and at any public postsecondary institution, plus preference on equal terms for aid, scholarships and other student benefits
eligibility: You are a Veteran who exhausted your federal education benefits without being able to finish a bachelor's or postgraduate course of study already begun, because the studies run longer than the period federal law authorises
Or you are a Veteran who has no education benefits at all under legislation passed by the Congress of the United States
In the second case you must maintain the academic standards the institution sets, and those standards cannot be more onerous than the academic requirements set for regular students
The degree concentration you finally choose does not matter
details: The second route is the remarkable one. A Veteran who never had federal education benefits is entitled to free tuition at Puerto Rico's public institutions on the same footing as one who used them up. Very few jurisdictions do that.

The documentation rule is a protection you can hold the institution to. To receive the benefit it is enough to present evidence of having served in the Armed Forces of the United States and of Veteran status under Article 5 of the law, a copy of valid photo identification, and an original certification from the federal Department of Veterans Affairs showing whether your federal education benefits are exhausted or about to be. The statute then says the University of Puerto Rico, all its academic units and any public higher education institution are barred from requiring other documentation as a precondition. If you are asked for more, point at this.

You also get preference, on equal terms, for the aid, scholarships and other benefits granted to students of the institution. The economic benefit can never exceed what would be granted for study at any higher education institution in Puerto Rico.

If you study at a recognised private or non-UPR institution in Puerto Rico, you are entitled to an amount for tuition plus stipends for books, library, laboratory, health plan and other items, capped at what that institution ordinarily charges other students for the same things for similar studies. The institution must be recognised by the Council on Higher Education or by a United States national accrediting agency.

The law names the institutions that must honour these rights, and the list goes well beyond the main university: the Conservatory of Music of Puerto Rico, the Puerto Rico Technological Institute of the Department of Education and its campuses, the School of Plastic Arts and Design, the School of Die and Tool Making, the San Juan University College and the Criminal Justice University College at Gurabo.

Family members are covered in defined cases. A non-resident spouse or child using the Veteran's transferred Montgomery or Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits qualifies if they enroll in the public institution within three years of the Veteran's discharge, after 90 days or more of active military service. A non-resident surviving spouse or child on the Fry Scholarship qualifies if they enroll within three years of the Veteran's death in the line of duty, after 90 days or more of active service.
The Secretary of Education is authorised to make rules, with the Governor's approval, so ask about current procedure as well as the statute.
agency: University of Puerto Rico and the public postsecondary institutions, with rules from the Secretary of Education
statuteRef: Ley 203-2007, Article B, rights relating to education
